PostgreSQL 19 Released (via) Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.
This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.
In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();
That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';
The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.
I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.
Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Mark Gurman, reporting for Bloomberg today (gift link):

Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight
years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the
matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying
technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their
pictures and video.

Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s
exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his
responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who
asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An
Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the
iPhone 17 lineup last year.

I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were all good. It was never “Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.

McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned Center Stage selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was the public face for that feature — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and according to McCormack himself, over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones every day. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of billions of people is significant; McCormack understood that.

But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: Patterns: Art of the Natural World. He discussed the book in an hour-long interview with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose job title is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also a talented photographer.)
Gurman:

His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a
fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet
Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly
embraced generative AI features that allow users to make
substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction
between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.

Two years ago in his iPhone 16 Pro review, returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, quoted Patel quoting McCormack, and added:

McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply
with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the
conservative company when it comes to generative AI and
photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not
complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it
personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves
significant use of generative AI.

This year, Apple added “extend” and “reframe” alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t hate them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.

Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features into the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was great at keeping stupid ideas out of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.
Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.

Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need.

Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or texting it.

Google first introduced its Spark AI agent in May, but it was only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The launch of tasks in Gemini brings Spark’s capabilities to all users in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia, and India. You can find tasks by opening Gemini and changing the toggle on the homepage from “Chat” to “Tasks.”

Tasks in Gemini is just one of the many agentic AI features that have emerged over the past year, including Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots, and Meta’s Muse. Google says Gemini will perform tasks in a “hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users.” You can also provide instructions for Gemini while it completes tasks. When performing more sensitive tasks, like purchasing an item, it will stop working and ask for your permission before following through.

How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.

That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.

At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.
Image: Rockstar Games

Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.

Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.
Image: Rockstar Games

What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.

The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.

To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.

There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.
Image: Rockstar Games

All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.

Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.

But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.

It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.

Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience

I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.

You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.

Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.
Image: Rockstar Games

It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.

Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.

To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.

For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.

Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.
Image: Rockstar Games

What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.

The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.

To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.

There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.
Image: Rockstar Games

All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.

Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.

But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.

It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.

Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience

I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.

You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.

Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.
Image: Rockstar Games

It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.

Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.

To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.

For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

blocks.text: One thing people complained about most on Stack Overflow was having their questions closed and marked as duplicates of other questions that were only slightly related. The poster would argue in the comments, trying to make the case that their question was different, only for it to fall on deaf ears.

Then LLMs came along and ate Stack Overflow's lunch. An LLM will answer your question, and with even more vigor if a related question exists online. Everyone was happy, until the LLMs suddenly stopped responding.

Along the way, we decided that LLMs are too dangerous and shouldn't answer every development question. If your prompt sounds, even vaguely, like you are trying to circumvent security, the model drops your request and flags your account. Do it enough times, and your account is closed for good.
Now it's no longer smug developers closing questions. You are left with an unanswered prompt and no one to pin the fault on.
Even when they don't blatantly stop you in your tracks, the answers can feel gated, as if the model knows the answer but deliberately won't tell you.

Now, I was never so much against marking questions as duplicates. In the majority of cases I encountered, the person asking could have benefited from reading the original question. You don't get a full answer, but it serves as a guide that helps you find a solution. With LLMs withholding answers, the fix is often to pay for a more expensive model. So maybe it's not so much Stack Overflow as ExpertSexChange that is back.

How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (permalink)

There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists.

After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, poorer than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are much, much richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined.

This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving power.

If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain with is just giving them more to bargain away.

I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY!

This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat.

If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the structure of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change.

There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called Chokepoint Capitalism, and we devoted half of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses:
https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

We got really excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies:
https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708

Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits.

Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically most vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing terrible deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal.

Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, but the creators of those works are entitled to even less of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them.

Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator.

Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can still exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally can't promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing.

That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller The Bezzle, where I use this as a key plot point:
https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/

Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on much more favorable terms. Just the threat of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby:
https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/

In Chokepoint Capitalism, Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, except the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination.

But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork.

Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to take it away from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire

Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists":
https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037
With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress.

Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer.

Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips.

This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios).

Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer.

You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does not apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos).

The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years.

Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster Heat, and New Regency, the studio that released it:
https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/

Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to Heat. But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others":
https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/

This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way
It let the Spinal Tap crew get a much better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) Spinal Tap II:
https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087

The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get The Matrix back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through:
https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix

This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants.
It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies.

In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you. The Authors Alliance is a nonprofit that defends the rights of authors (I volunteer for its advisory board); we've got a free online tool that will help you terminate your own transfers and get your rights back:
https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/

How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (permalink)

There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists.

After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, poorer than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are much, much richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined.

This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving power.

If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain with is just giving them more to bargain away.

I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY!

This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat.

If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the structure of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change.

There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called Chokepoint Capitalism, and we devoted half of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses:
https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

We got really excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies:
https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708

Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits.

Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically most vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing terrible deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal.

Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, but the creators of those works are entitled to even less of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them.

Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator.

Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can still exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally can't promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing.

That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller The Bezzle, where I use this as a key plot point:
https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/

Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on much more favorable terms. Just the threat of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby:
https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/

In Chokepoint Capitalism, Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, except the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination.

But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork.

Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to take it away from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire

Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists":
https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037
With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress.

Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer.

Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips.

This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios).

Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer.

You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does not apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos).

The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years.

Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster Heat, and New Regency, the studio that released it:
https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/

Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to Heat. But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others":
https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/

This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way
It let the Spinal Tap crew get a much better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) Spinal Tap II:
https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087

The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get The Matrix back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through:
https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix

This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants.
It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies.

In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you. The Authors Alliance is a nonprofit that defends the rights of authors (I volunteer for its advisory board); we've got a free online tool that will help you terminate your own transfers and get your rights back:
https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/

blocks.text: Close quarters battle opera! The full force of two very talented singers blasted directly at an audience sat mere centimetres from the stage, and ricocheting around the tiny venue.
This was a free showing of a brand new opera based on the play by Tabitha Hayward.

Daniella Sicari and Lucy Gibbs are ridiculously talented - but I think the score is perhaps a little too basic to do them justice. There's not a great deal melody, just an endless warble of sing-speaking. It ends up feeling a mite repetitive - which shouldn't really happen in a one-act show.

The accordionist, Alise Siliņa, is incredible. She was able to conjure a whole soundscape from a single instrument. More than just music, she provided surreal sound effects and a true air of delirium. Having live accompaniment make such a positive difference to these sorts of shows.

The opera is about teenage histrionics which, when multiplied by the natural exuberance of opera, make the show almost unbearably intense. There are a lot of plot elements stuffed in to the 75 minute running time. Ghosts! Teenage pregnancy! BFF breakups! Sibling rivalries! Tragedy! It becomes difficult to keep up with what is being sung. And yet the show does drag on a touch. Just when you think it has reached a natural climax, it finds a new diversion to explore.
It is great that new operas are still being works hoped, developed, and performed. There is a lot to like about FORT, but I think it tries to pack in too much into too small a space.

blocks.text: A word is universal if it contains every permutation of its alphabet as a subsequence: the letters must appear in order, but gaps are allowed.

For example, you can find all six permutations of the digits 1, 2, and 3 inside the string 1231213. Not all permutations can be found as a contiguous substring—that would be a superpermutation—but all can be found as a subsequence.
The word

is universal for the set of 10 digits. This word was discovered some time ago, but Jason Davies has recently proved that this the smallest universal word on 10 digits. It has 83 characters, and Davies proved that no word of 82 characters is universal over the digits. See his paper here.
I’m surprised that all 10! = 3,628,800 permutations of 10 digits can be found as subsequences of such a relatively short word.

Universal words, or supersequences, are easily confused with superpermutations. See OEIS sequences A062714 and A180632. Minimal length superpermutations are necessarily longer than minimal length supersequences [1] since the requirements on the former are stricter, requiring permutations to appear as contiguous substrings and not merely as subsequences. In other words, every superpermutation is a supersequence, but not vice versa.

blocks.text: Today, as Anthropic’s AI takes over the stock market, it’s more than a little weird to write a little lament to the way the internet once was.
But we recently lost Salon, one of the few news sites that’s been here more or less the entire time. And the reason cited sounds quite familiar:

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.

I’m sure that’s certainly true. But I also know that Salon has likely hit more of those road bumps than most. When it started, it was a site build around news, yes, but also a robust comments section. Then it gave that up, willingly. As I wrote in an aside earlier this year:

A testament to its legacy: Salon used the software as the anchor of its digital community for more than 15 years, only shutting it down in 2011 out of concerns it wasn’t where the Web was going. With another 15 years of retrospect, can we argue that this was probably a bad move? Perhaps.

I don’t want to argue prescience, but I do think decisions like these, where we handed off the infrastructure of our own destines to other companies in hopes that maybe they’d have a better idea than we would? They ultimately cost us necessary momentum and foundational strength.

The thing is, media outlets like Salon, which got its initial seed funding from Apple and Adobe (and Adobe continued to financially support for years after its launch), have long been swimming upstream. It had to ride a series of technology trends (search, social, video) to stay afloat. It wasn’t like Salon had originated any of these; it had to survive on the back of a tech ecosystem that saw financial opportunity in journalism, but not enough to build around it forever.

(It’s not like Adobe has invested millions of dollars in Salon anytime recently, after all. Free idea, Adobe: Maybe do that. Would be a great goodwill opportunity, considering the creatives you’ve frustrated of late.)

Matt Wolfbridge, the editor of the great Typebar Magazine which I’ve contributed to in the past, wrote a loving, but honest, take about where Salon went. He arrived there after its initial heyday, the period that gave us Joan Walsh and later Glenn Greenwald. While he was there, he grew its social presence in a big way. He didn’t hide its flaws, but he did note how much he loved the thing:

Everyone was happy for me when I did leave Salon for a surging news startup, which I did with a degree of sadness. Salon was the first thing in my professional life that had ever gone right. And it was staffed by many brilliant people whose devotion to the written word was so great they put up with the ownership’s demands. I am grateful for the time I spent there.
I didn’t work at Salon. I can’t claim any sort of institutional knowledge of what was there, like Matt can. But what I can say is that stuff like this makes me endlessly sad.
Salon’s late-stage owner: A reflection of 31 years of pivots?

Salon, in its own way, has reflected all the good and bad trends of digital-first journalism over the past 31 years. The most recent trend it reflected? The weird owner nobody who ever of, taking it over, Bending Spoons-style.

That’s right, Salon went down the same road that another great site in the internet’s digital legacy, Deadspin, did. It, too, was sold to a company based in Malta, with a background in iGaming, the shorthand term for “online gambling.” Salon, whatever its qualities before this shutdown happened, stuck out like a sore thumb in the context of Find.co’s product catalog.

“Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto” is not something one would associate with a long-running publication. But when I read “company that has crypto and iGaming interests buys website with 31 years of SEO juice,” I think to myself, “Oh, they want the Google ranking, not the outlet.”
I could be wrong. Maybe the Find.co folks are perfectly nice people who thought it’d be fun to make a bet on traditional journalism at a time when it seems like nobody else was.

But given the way that media brands get put through the wringer by both internal and external technology partners, it’s not hard to look at situations like these with a raised eyebrow. After all, today it’s Salon. Tomorrow, it could be another legendary site. The problem with building empires on the shared infrastructure of others is that they’re changing the infrastructure even if you don’t want them to. You’re forced to react to it at all times.

And sometimes, those companies don’t even know what the hell they’re doing, either. I’ve been following the recent SEO-website headlines with great interest after it came out that Google’s AI Mode, a search feature that the company heavily pushed onto its search engine, was less profitable than the old version of Google. And that has led Google to test minimizing it in searches. (Unfortunately, that doesn’t include the much-maligned AI overviews, but hey, at least &udm=14 exists.)

That’s telling. Like the infamous Facebook-driven pivot to video that was based on inflated data, an entire industry has been forced to leap based on bets that another company is making without knowing that what they’re doing is actually working.
What a legendary Wawa can teach you about top-down decision-making

Recently, I was on the home page of The Virginian-Pilot, a paper where I once helped start a free daily newspaper, reading about how a community was protesting in an attempt to save a beloved Wawa location. The story I think offers a neat parallel for the challenges journalism faces. This location meant a lot to the students of William & Mary, but Wawa wants more stores with attached gas stations. Classic example of making a 30,000-foot decision without looking at what’s happening on the ground.

The tech industry is full of decisions like these, where bold bets are made at a high level without understanding where the value equation actually lies. Our latest initiative requires us to strategically pivot towards gas stations, so we must stop serving 19-year-olds who want a hoagie in the middle of the night. We need to push people towards AI so we keep them on site longer, so we hurt all the symbiotic relationships we created over the past 30 years.
At the bottom of the Pilot article, my eye was drawn to the fine print, presumably put there by the Tribune bosses:

The use of any content on this website for the purpose of training artificial intelligence systems, algorithms, machine learning models, text and data mining, or similar use is strictly prohibited without explicit written consent.

We are now past the point where media outlets are going to be nice about it. They’ve been burned way too many times. This top-down stuff is gonna cost us everything we actually care about if we don’t stop it.

Listen, as lawyers go, Lowell “The Hammer” Stanley is as close as you’ll find to a real-life Saul Goodman. Which is why it’s shocking to learn that, like Goodman infamously once did, Stanley just had his law license suspended.

Just wanted to offer a quick shout to zsKnight, the developer of ZSNES, who has made an utterly charming game collection called Retro Endurance 8 Bit. The gimmick: The game keeps changing, channel-clicker style, as you rush through levels. (Think Action 52/UFO 50, but with a quirky sense of humor all its own.) Find it on Steam here.
